The main optimality theorem applies to exact minimax polynomials with known singular-value intervals, while the practical algorithm uses guessed lower bounds, Frobenius normalization, cushioning, and safety rescaling; the theory only partially explains the implemented method.

Reproducibility is weaker than it should be: the reproducibility statement has an incomplete source-code location, and there are apparent inconsistencies between Algorithm 1 and Implementation 1 around normalization and numerical safety constants.
The strongest application evidence is concentrated on GPT-2/FineWeb and Muon-specific baselines; broader LLM scales, architectures, optimizers, and tasks would make the impact claims more convincing.
The CIFAR experiments are mixed and explicitly do not show a consistent advantage for Polar Express, suggesting the practical benefit may be narrower than the general framing implies.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant bottleneck in Muon-style optimization: fast GPU-friendly approximation of the polar factor using only matrix multiplications.
The minimax/composite-polynomial framing is clear, and the greedy optimality result gives a clean theoretical justification for the proposed update sequence under the stated interval assumptions.

The method is simple to implement, includes explicit PyTorch-style code and precomputed coefficients, and is plausibly useful as a drop-in replacement for existing Newton-Schulz/Jordan/You-style Muon updates.

The empirical section is broader than many optimizer papers: it includes synthetic convergence, GPT-2 gradient matrices, GPT-2 Small/Large training on 1B and 10B FineWeb tokens, weight-decay ablations, SVD/iteration-count ablations, and some vision experiments.
The paper is generally well written and does a reasonable job connecting numerical linear algebra, approximation theory, and modern deep learning optimizer practice.
weaknesses: The central optimality claim applies to an idealized exact-arithmetic minimax problem with known spectral interval, while the actual algorithm used in experiments introduces cushioning, safety scaling, guessed lower bounds, and bfloat16 heuristics. The gap between theorem and deployed method is significant.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to adaptive polynomial/rational sign iterations, Chen and Chow, Zolotarev/Nakatsukasa-Freund style methods, and related composite-polynomial work. The paper positions this reasonably, but the conceptual advance may be narrower than the title suggests.

The LLM training gains, especially at 10B tokens, are small and appear to be reported without multiple seeds or statistical uncertainty. This makes it hard to distinguish robust optimizer improvement from run-to-run noise or hyperparameter luck.
The ablation showing that exact SVD or many more Polar Express iterations do not improve Muon weakens the causal story that better polar approximation is the reason for better training performance.
The image classification experiments do not show a consistent advantage for Polar Express, and these less favorable results are mostly relegated to the appendix.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided: the source-code location appears blank, and important details such as random seeds, preprocessing, exact training code, and variance for expensive runs are not sufficiently specified.

Some implementation and presentation details reduce confidence, including inconsistencies between the algorithm text and code-level normalization, hard-coded coefficients, and minor algorithm/pseudocode typos.

strengths: Clear and timely contribution: the paper connects classical matrix sign/polar-decomposition algorithms to the practical needs of Muon-style neural network training, where low-precision GPU-friendly polynomial iterations matter.

The main theoretical result is meaningful: deriving greedy per-iteration minimax polynomial updates and proving global optimality for the composed approximation under the stated spectral-interval model gives the method a stronger foundation than recent heuristic coefficient searches.
The method is simple and practical: the online implementation is short, dependency-light, uses only matrix multiplications, and directly targets bfloat16 deployment.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this niche: synthetic convergence, GPT-2 Small/Large on 1B tokens, selected 10B-token runs, weight-decay ablations, iteration-count/SVD ablations, and image-classification experiments.
The paper is unusually honest about where improvements are small or absent, especially on CIFAR/ViT settings and at longer GPT-2 training horizons.
weaknesses: The empirical gains, while consistent in the main GPT-2 runs, are often modest, especially at 10B tokens, and large-scale runs appear to lack multiple random seeds or uncertainty estimates.

The strongest theoretical optimality claims apply to the idealized exact-arithmetic interval problem, whereas the implemented method uses cushioning, safety rescaling, guessed lower bounds, and finite-precision modifications; the gap is discussed but not fully characterized theoretically.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to Chen & Chow, Nakatsukasa/Freund, and related composite-polynomial/sign-approximation work; the paper’s value is in synthesis, proof, and deep-learning validation rather than a wholly new algorithmic paradigm.

Comparisons could be stronger: the paper does not deeply benchmark against all relevant stabilized/scaled polynomial variants or rational methods in carefully controlled wall-clock regimes, even if the motivation for excluding rational methods is plausible.

Reproducibility is decent through code snippets, but the experimental code/link in the reproducibility statement appears incomplete in the manuscript text, and many expensive training details would benefit from a more explicit artifact checklist.
